passage: 'Parveen, you asked why I've stopped replying at 2 am. Okay, so. In the summer holidays I was on my phone till three most nights, videos, one after another. I'd tell myself, one more, and suddenly it was light outside. School started and I was falling asleep in first period. Our class teacher actually asked if everything was okay at home, which was so embarrassing. So I made rules. Phone charges in the kitchen from ten-thirty. I bought an old alarm clock from the market for eighty rupees. The first three nights I lay there itching to check it. Now I read for a bit and I'm asleep before eleven. I'm not perfect. Sundays I still slip. But my mornings feel like mine again.'

qa.q: How much did Hafsa pay for the alarm clock?
qa.a: Eighty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa find the teacher's question embarrassing?
qa.a: It showed her tiredness was obvious to adults, and she felt ashamed that her late nights looked like trouble at home.

qa.q: What could help Hafsa on the Sundays when she slips?
qa.a: She could keep the phone-in-the-kitchen rule on weekends too, or ask a family member to remind her gently.

qa.q: How might Parveen be affected by Hafsa's new routine?
qa.a: She loses her late-night chat partner, but may also feel nudged to look at her own habits.

grounding: Shows a teenager replacing late-night screen use with simple rules that protect her sleep and school mornings.

passage: I'm Sudha, Kavitha's cousin, and we share a room when she stays over on weekends. This month I noticed a few things. She used to scroll in bed till late; now her phone sits on my desk after ten, and she lays out her school clothes before sleeping. Last Saturday some older boys from the colony were smoking behind the water tank and called her over. I was on the terrace and saw her shake her head, laugh, and keep walking to the shop. When she came up, she didn't mention it. She just said, 'I'm doing the morning run with Papa tomorrow, wake me at six.' I don't know if saying no was hard for her. She didn't look like it. But she did take the long way home.

qa.q: Where were the older boys smoking?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: What might Kavitha taking the long way home suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she wanted to avoid the boys, even if saying no looked easy, though Sudha can't be sure.

qa.q: How could Kavitha's family support these new habits?
qa.a: They could keep up the morning runs with Papa, notice her routines, and stay someone she can talk to if the pressure grows.

qa.q: How does Sudha seem to feel about the change in Kavitha?
qa.a: She seems quietly impressed and a little curious, noticing the changes without asking directly.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager keeping healthy routines and turning away from a substance risk, seen by her cousin.

passage:
Dear Nandini,
Big week here. On Tuesday I found a wallet near the bus stop with four thousand rupees and a driving licence in it. My first thought, honestly, was that I could buy those headphones. Then I thought of Dadaji; everyone in our lane calls him 'the man who never kept a paisa that wasn't his.' I didn't want to be the one who broke that. So Papa and I took it to the police station. I was nervous, but the constable was kind. He showed me the register where they log found property and explained that the owner has to show ID to claim it. The owner, an old tailor, called on Thursday and cried on the phone. Dadaji didn't say much. He just put his hand on my head at dinner.
Miss you,
Hansa

qa.q: How much money was in the wallet?
qa.a: Four thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Hansa think of Dadaji when she found the wallet?
qa.a: She valued the family name for honesty that he built and didn't want to be the one to break it.

qa.q: What did Hansa's family get right in how they handled the wallet?
qa.a: Papa went with her to the police station, so she learned the proper legal process instead of handling it alone.

qa.q: How might the tailor have felt when he got the call?
qa.a: Deeply relieved and grateful, which is why he cried on the phone.

grounding: Shows a teenager acting to uphold her family's good name and following the lawful process for found property.

passage: 'Jeevan, you'll laugh, but the most interesting thing I did this holiday was stand in a queue at the municipal office. Papa had to pay the house tax, and he made me come. I was sulking. Then the clerk showed me the receipt, and there was this line: part of it goes to the ward's water and drains. I asked him, so if people don't pay, the drains near our school just stay broken? He said, "More or less." That stuck with me. Now I notice things, the new streetlight, the park gate. I read the ward notice board for the first time. Papa says his father used to say paying on time is part of our family's respect. I used to think that was just old talk.'

qa.q: Where did Yash stand in a queue?
qa.a: At the municipal office.

qa.q: What does 'That stuck with me' suggest about how Yash's thinking changed?
qa.a: He began to see taxes as tied to things he uses, like drains and streetlights, instead of a boring chore.

qa.q: What could Yash do next to act on this new interest?
qa.a: He could keep reading the ward notice board or attend a ward meeting with Papa to see how decisions are made.

qa.q: How might Papa feel hearing Yash talk this way?
qa.a: Probably pleased, since he made Yash come along and the family value is finally making sense to him. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a teenager starting to understand civic duties like taxes and linking them to family respect.

passage: 'Tanvir, you asked what I learned this year. Okay, one night. Somebody posted a video mocking our football team, and one of the players was my cousin. I typed a reply full of abuse, really nasty stuff about the guy's family. My thumb was on send. Then I thought: this will be online forever, with my name on it, and colleges look at this stuff. And Abbu would see it. I deleted it. Instead I messaged my cousin privately: "Ignore him, you played well." Next day I reported the video. That's it. Not dramatic. But I learned there's a gap between feeling something and posting it, and I have to live in that gap.'

qa.q: Who was the player in the mocked video?
qa.a: Asif's cousin.

qa.q: What was Asif worried about when his thumb was on send?
qa.a: He worried the comment would stay online with his name, affect how colleges see him, and that Abbu would see it.

qa.q: Which of Asif's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Messaging his cousin privately and reporting the video, because it supported his cousin and dealt with the post without adding more abuse.

qa.q: How might Asif's cousin have felt getting his private message?
qa.a: Comforted and backed up, without being dragged into a public fight.

grounding: Shows a teenager protecting his reputation and choosing ethical online behaviour over an abusive reply.

passage: I'm Bidisha, and I sit next to Deepika. Here's what I've seen this term. She leaves at 1:30 on Wednesdays because she takes her Nani to her check-ups, and she copies the missed notes from me that evening without fail. When our class group started a poll ranking girls by looks, almost everyone voted, and I did too. Deepika posted one line: 'Not voting on people. Leaving this group.' Then she left. Some people called her dramatic. The next day the class teacher found out and the poll was deleted; I don't know if Deepika told her. When I asked, she just shrugged. 'I have Nani's appointments and physics. No time for that stuff.' I think it bothered her more than she said. Her ears were red.

qa.q: What time does Deepika leave on Wednesdays?
What might Deepika's red ears suggest about her shrug?
qa.a: They suggest the poll and people's reactions bothered her more than her casual words showed.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do now that she has seen Deepika's stand?
qa.a: She could take back her own vote and tell Deepika she agrees, or tell a teacher if such polls start again.

qa.q: How might the girls ranked in the poll have been affected?
qa.a: They could feel judged and hurt by classmates; Deepika's refusal showed at least one person wouldn't take part.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager keeping family and study duties while refusing to join online bullying, seen by a classmate.

passage: 'Binita, okay, confession. First month in Bengaluru, I ran out of money on the nineteenth. No idea where it went. So I sat with my bank messages and a notebook for a whole Sunday. Rent, electricity, mess fee, fine. Then thirty-one food deliveries. Thirty-one! And three subscriptions I forgot I'd started. I felt sick, honestly. I didn't want to call home for money; Appa's already stretched. So now, the day my stipend comes, rent and bills go out first. What's left I keep in envelopes, actual cash, one for each week. When a week's envelope is empty, I cook rice and eggs. It's boring. But last month I had eleven hundred left over, and I didn't have to ask anyone.'

qa.q: On which date did Siddharth run out of money in his first month?
qa.a: The nineteenth.

qa.q: Why didn't Siddharth want to call home for money?
qa.a: He felt his father was already stretched and he wanted to manage on his own.

qa.q: What part of Siddharth's system could a friend like Binita copy, and why?
qa.a: Paying rent and bills first on stipend day, because it protects the essentials before other spending.

qa.q: How might Appa feel if he learned about Siddharth's system?
qa.a: Relieved and proud that his son is handling money on his own.

grounding: Shows a young adult tracking his spending and setting up his own budget without parents overseeing it.

passage: I'm Vandana. I share a flat in Pune with Shreya, and I've watched her change since June. At first, bills just piled up on the fridge. The electricity got cut once, for a whole evening, because a payment slipped. She didn't cry, but she went very quiet and sat on the floor with a calculator. Now there's a whiteboard by the door with every due date and a tick beside each. She splits the internet bill with me on the first, exact to the rupee, and shows me the receipt. Last week her parents offered to send extra, and I heard her say, 'No, Mummy, I've got it this month.' I don't know if she was sure. She checked the whiteboard twice after the call.

qa.q: Where is the whiteboard?
qa.a: By the door.

qa.q: What might Shreya checking the whiteboard twice after the call suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she was not fully sure she could manage, even though she wanted to handle it herself.

qa.q: What could help Shreya if a month gets tight?
qa.a: She could keep tracking dues and, if money runs short, talk honestly with her parents rather than letting bills slip.

qa.q: How does Vandana benefit from Shreya's new system?
qa.a: Bills are split on time and shown clearly, so there is less stress and no more surprise power cuts.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult learning to pay bills and manage expenses on her own, seen by her flatmate.

passage:
Kavitha: SOS. washed my white kurta with the new red dupatta
Wasim: oh no. pink?
Kavitha: very pink 😢
Wasim: welcome to living alone. separate colours next time
Kavitha: i know that NOW
Wasim: also what did u eat today
Kavitha: biscuits. and tea. twice
Wasim: kavitha.
Kavitha: i was going to make dal but the pressure cooker scares me
Wasim: come over sunday. i'll show u. it's just whistles, not a bomb
Kavitha: ok. i'll bring vegetables
Kavitha: also i swept and mopped the whole room today. first time in 3 weeks 😅
Wasim: progress! 👍

qa.q: What did Kavitha wash her white kurta with?
qa.a: The new red dupatta.

qa.q: Why hadn't Kavitha made the dal?
qa.a: She felt scared of using the pressure cooker.

qa.q: What makes Wasim's offer a helpful way to support her?
qa.a: He will show her in person on Sunday, so she learns the skill herself rather than him doing it for her.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Kavitha's first weeks living alone?
qa.a: He seems amused but caring, teasing her while checking that she eats properly.

grounding: Shows a young adult struggling with laundry, cooking and cleaning on her own and starting to learn.

passage: When his mother Rajni left for two weeks to look after his grandmother, Vikas, nineteen, had their house in the kasba to himself for the first time. The first morning he burned the rotis and ate them anyway, standing by the stove. By day three he had found a rhythm: fill the water drums before the supply stopped at eight, soak the clothes while the rice cooked, hang them on the roof before the sun got fierce. When the kitchen tap started leaking, he didn't call the plumber from the market; he watched the neighbour uncle do it once and changed the washer himself. On the phone, his mother asked if he was eating. 'Dal, rice, bhindi,' he said, a little proud. 'The rotis are still shaped like maps.'

qa.q: By what time did the water supply stop?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: What does 'a little proud' in Vikas's reply suggest?
qa.a: He felt pleased with himself for running the house alone, while being honest about his rotis.

qa.q: What could Vikas do to keep improving before his mother returns?
qa.a: He could practise rotis daily and write down the routine that works, so it lasts after she is back.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel hearing his reply on the phone?
qa.a: Relieved he is eating properly and amused by his joke, maybe proud of how he is coping. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young adult managing cooking, laundry and small repairs on his own in a small-town home.

passage:
Dear Naveen Sir,
You used to say college would be 'freedom with a hidden bill.' I get it now. In my first semester I had classes only in the mornings and nothing after two. No bells, no one checking. I slept through afternoons, watched series, and told myself I'd study 'in the evening.' The evening kept moving. I nearly failed the statistics mid-term. After that I sat down and made my day into a timetable I set for myself: library from three to five, a walk at six, calls home at nine. I even put in a 'lazy hour', so I'd stop feeling guilty about resting. It isn't perfect, but I passed the finals with a B. I wanted you to know your line stayed with me.
Regards,
Sharmila

qa.q: What grade did Sharmila get in the finals?
qa.a: A B.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila add a 'lazy hour' to her timetable?
qa.a: She wanted to rest without feeling guilty, so she could stick to the rest of her plan.

qa.q: What would you advise a new college student based on Sharmila's letter?
qa.a: Build your own timetable early, with fixed study blocks and planned rest, before a bad test forces it.

qa.q: How might Naveen Sir feel reading this?
qa.a: Touched and pleased that his warning stayed with her and helped. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to structure open college hours once no bells or parents set her schedule.

passage: 'Mehak, you keep asking how I get anything done working from home. Honestly, the first two months I didn't. I'd wake at ten, check messages in bed, and suddenly it was lunch and I hadn't drawn a line. No boss, no office. So I stole the school idea: bells. I set three alarms. Nine, work starts, and I get dressed like I'm going out. One, lunch away from the desk. Five, stop, no matter what. In between, I list only three tasks on a sticky note, not twenty. Some days it falls apart. A client calls, my cousin drops in. But I finished the book cover two days early last week, and I actually had Sunday free. That felt like a small miracle.'

qa.q: How many alarms does Charu set?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What does Charu mean when she calls her free Sunday 'a small miracle'?
qa.a: She felt surprised and relieved that her new structure gave her real free time after months of drifting.

qa.q: What could Charu try on days when her plan falls apart?
qa.a: She could pick just one of her three tasks to finish and start fresh the next morning, instead of giving up on the week.

qa.q: How might Charu's clients see the change?
qa.a: They would notice work arriving on time or early, which builds their trust in her.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult creating her own daily structure to replace the bells and supervision she no longer has.

passage: In the laundry room of her residence in Montreal, Rania, nineteen, held the form due on Friday: declare your major. She had taken intro psychology, economics and an art elective, and liked them all a little. Her roommate Camila folded towels beside her. 'Which one made you forget to eat?' Rania thought. It wasn't any of the classes. It was her weekend job at the bike co-op, rebuilding wheels, where three hours felt like ten minutes. 'That's not a major.' 'The college has a mechanical technology program,' Camila said. 'Two years. Hands-on.' Rania's stomach flipped: fear of disappointing her parents, and something like relief. That night she emailed the program advisor. On Friday she handed in the form with a new name written in.

qa.q: When was the form due?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Rania have when Camila mentioned the program?
qa.a: She felt afraid of disappointing her parents and also relieved, as if a real fit had been named.

qa.q: What could Rania do to feel surer about her choice?
qa.a: She could talk with the advisor and current students, and explain her reasons to her parents calmly.

qa.q: How might Rania's parents react to her new path?
qa.a: They might be surprised or worried at first, but could come round if they see how committed and happy she is.

grounding: Shows a young adult committing to a specific hands-on program after noticing where her real absorption lies.

passage: The electrical workshop at the ITI smelled of hot solder and dust. Kiran, twenty, finished wiring the practice board and flicked the switch; all four bulbs lit. Vijay Sir, the instructor, nodded but didn't smile. 'Your cousins are all doing BCom, no?' 'Yes, sir.' 'And you?' Kiran wiped his hands. For a year he had been half in, half out, thinking he might switch to a degree once the relatives stopped asking. 'I want the wireman licence,' he said. 'Then solar installation. I'm not switching.' He was surprised how steady his voice sounded. Vijay Sir finally smiled and handed him the form for the advanced solar module. 'Then stop coming late on Mondays.' Kiran laughed. 'Yes, sir.'

qa.q: How many bulbs lit when Kiran flicked the switch?
qa.a: All four.

qa.q: What did Kiran notice about his own voice, and what does it show about how he felt?
qa.a: He was surprised it sounded steady, which shows he felt sure of his choice after a year of doubt.

qa.q: How did Vijay Sir support Kiran's commitment?
qa.a: He gave him the form for the advanced module and also held him to a standard about punctuality.

qa.q: How might Kiran's relatives see his choice?
qa.a: Some may compare him with the cousins doing BCom, but they may come to respect a skilled trade.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult committing to a specific trade path at a training institute.

passage:
Dear Vikas,
Thank you for the list you sent in March. I want to tell you where I am. After my BA, all I had was 'good communication skills', which every form asks for and nobody believes. So I picked the thing on your list that scared me most: spreadsheets and data cleaning. Evenings for four months. First a free online course through the library, then real practice on my uncle's shop accounts, which were a mess. I cried once over a formula that wouldn't work. Last week I did a test task for a small logistics company, and they've called me for a second round. I'm not an expert. But now when I say I can do something, I can show it.
Warmly,
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dilnaz practise on?
qa.a: Her uncle's shop accounts.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz pick spreadsheets from the list?
qa.a: It was the skill that scared her most, and she wanted something concrete to show instead of vague claims.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do before the second round?
qa.a: Prepare a short example of her shop-accounts work and practise explaining how she solved a problem.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel reading this update?
qa.a: Glad and proud that his list turned into real progress, and trusted as a mentor.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from a general degree to a specific, provable professional skill.

passage: 'Disha, remember when I said I'd just do an MBA like everyone? Yeah, no. After BCom I took a six-month baking course at a small institute in Lucknow. Day one I thought I knew cakes; I'd been baking at home for years. Then the chef made me weigh everything to the gram and throw out three batches of bread because the dough was underworked. My arms hurt for a week. But slowly it clicked. Temperature, timing, why a recipe fails. Last month I did my first paid order, a wedding, two hundred cupcakes, and I didn't panic. Home baking was a hobby. This is a skill I can sell. It feels different in my hands.'

qa.q: How long was Noor's baking course?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: What does 'It feels different in my hands' suggest about how Noor sees herself now?
qa.a: She feels like a skilled professional rather than a hobbyist, with new confidence in her work.

qa.q: What would you advise Noor to do next?
qa.a: Keep taking paid orders and note what goes right and wrong each time, perhaps learning one advanced technique.

qa.q: How might Disha see Noor's change of plans?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since Noor had planned an MBA, but impressed by how seriously she has trained. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young adult turning a hobby into a trained, marketable skill after general studies.

passage: The alumni meet in the college auditorium in Delhi was loud, and Divyansh, twenty-one, stood by the snacks table holding a paper cup for twenty minutes. He had printed three copies of his CV, and they were going soft in his bag. Then he saw Deepika, a senior from four batches ahead who now worked at a water-treatment firm he had read about. He walked over before he could stop himself. 'Ma'am, sorry, I read your project on low-cost filters. Could I ask how you got into that field?' She laughed. 'Deepika, please. Not ma'am.' They talked for ten minutes. She told him about a summer internship nobody applied to because it was in a small town. 'Email me tonight. Mention the filters.' He did, at 11:40 pm, after four drafts.

qa.q: How many copies of his CV had Divyansh printed?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What does Divyansh standing by the snacks table for twenty minutes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous and shy about approaching people.

qa.q: Which of Divyansh's choices helped the conversation work?
qa.a: Mentioning her actual project showed genuine interest, which made her willing to help.

qa.q: How might Deepika have seen Divyansh's approach?
qa.a: She probably liked that he had read her work and was glad to help a junior who seemed sincere.

grounding: Shows a young adult making a first professional contact that opens an internship lead.

passage:
'Tanvir Mamu, can I ask you something awkward?'
'Those are my favourite.'
Jaya pushed her plate aside. 'You know people at architecture firms. I've applied to eleven internships online. Nothing.'
'And you want me to call someone.'
'No! I mean... I don't know what I want.'
He smiled. 'Here's what I can do. I'll introduce you to one person, my old classmate. Not to get you a job. To have tea and ask questions.'
'What questions?'
'What she wishes she'd known at twenty. What her firm looks for. Then you listen more than you talk.'
'And after?'
'After, you send a short thank-you message. And you don't ask for anything the first time.'
Jaya nodded slowly. 'That's harder than applying online.'
'Yes. It's also how most of us got our first break.'

qa.q: How many internships had Jaya applied to online?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: What does Jaya's 'I don't know what I want' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt awkward about asking for favours and unsure how to use her uncle's connections.

qa.q: What does Mamu's advice teach about early networking?
qa.a: Start with a genuine conversation, listen and say thanks, rather than asking for a job straight away.

qa.q: How might Mamu's classmate see a tea meeting like this?
qa.a: She would likely be happy to share advice with someone who comes to learn rather than to demand a job.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult learning, through family, how to build a first mentoring relationship in her field.

passage: The college innovation contest closed in forty-eight hours, and Bhupen's team had one idea that everyone agreed was boring. Then the hostel's power went out, taking the internet with it. Sitting in the dark corridor, Bhupen, an agriculture student from Assam, started talking about how his uncle could tell a sick tea bush by the buzzing around it. Ayesha, from the music department, sat up. 'Pests have sound signatures? We did frequency analysis in acoustics class.' They sketched in a notebook by torchlight: a cheap microphone on a stick, her way of sorting sounds, his knowledge of which insects matter. No money for parts, so they borrowed a phone's microphone for the demo. They submitted at 11:52 pm. It didn't win. But the agriculture professor asked them to keep working on it.

qa.q: How many hours were left before the contest closed?
qa.a: Forty-eight hours.

qa.q: What does Ayesha sitting up suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She suddenly felt excited, seeing how her acoustics knowledge could connect with Bhupen's story.

qa.q: What helped this team come up with an original idea?
qa.a: Mixing knowledge from two very different fields and taking a casual story seriously, rather than sticking with the safe idea.

qa.q: How might the agriculture professor have seen their project?
qa.a: As promising and original enough to develop further, even though it didn't win.

grounding: Shows young adults combining farming knowledge and acoustics into an original project under a tight deadline with no budget.

passage: In the cramped flat in Mumbai that she shared with Uma, Sonali, twenty-two, stared at the heap of fabric offcuts from her fashion course. Every semester they went in the bin. Uma, a civil engineering student, was complaining about her assignment: the classroom echoed, and foam panels were too expensive. Sonali held up a fistful of scraps. 'What if these are the panels?' Uma stopped. 'Compressed textile in frames. Actually, fibre does soak up sound.' They spent the weekend testing: a clapping test in the bathroom, with and without a panel of stitched denim scraps. Uma measured; Sonali played with colours so the panels looked like art. By Sunday night they had a prototype and a name scribbled on the fridge. Neither of them could have thought of it alone.

qa.q: Where did they test the panels?
qa.a: In the bathroom, with a clapping test.

qa.q: What does Uma stopping mid-complaint suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: She was struck by the idea and realised it might actually work, so her annoyance turned to interest.

qa.q: What could the pair do next with the prototype?
qa.a: Show it to teachers in both departments for feedback and test it in a real echoing room.

qa.q: What would change if Sonali and Uma had worked separately?
qa.a: Sonali's scraps would still be binned and Uma would still lack cheap panels; the idea came from combining both.

grounding: Illustrates young adults joining fashion and engineering knowledge to invent an original product.
